items.title: Cannibal Holocaust: The Movie That Made People Wonder If They Were Watching a Murder
items.author: Schill
items.content:
There are horror movies that scare you. There are horror movies that disgust you. There are horror movies that make you question the sanity of the people who made them.

Then there is .

Ruggero Deodato’s 1980 Italian exploitation film isn’t merely notorious because it contains graphic violence. Plenty of movies have blood, guts, torture, murder and other assorted reasons to lose your appetite. became infamous because it deliberately blurred the line between fiction and reality so effectively that people genuinely wondered whether they were watching an actual snuff film.

Deodato wanted the movie to feel real.

He succeeded so spectacularly that he ended up in court trying to prove that he hadn’t actually murdered his actors.

That’s an impressive amount of trouble to get into over a movie.

And just when you think the story can’t get any more disturbing, you discover that some of the animal deaths shown on screen were real.

So yes, is one of the most messed-up movies ever made.

But what makes it especially fascinating is that underneath all the gore, cannibalism, torture, exploitation and general cinematic depravity is an uncomfortable argument about the audience itself.

The movie isn’t just asking, “How much violence can you handle?”

Why do you want to watch it?

It Starts With a Missing Film Crew

The premise is deceptively simple.

A group of young American documentary filmmakers travels into the Amazon rainforest to make a documentary about supposedly primitive indigenous tribes.

A rescue team eventually locates their abandoned film equipment. The reels are brought back to New York, where anthropologist Harold Monroe is asked to examine the footage and figure out what happened.

This setup gives its most important structural trick.

The movie switches between traditional narrative filmmaking and the supposedly recovered documentary footage.

The footage becomes increasingly disturbing as Monroe watches it.

At first, the filmmakers appear to be brave journalists documenting a dangerous environment.

Then the truth becomes obvious.

They deliberately provoke the people they’re filming. They manipulate situations. They stage events. They destroy property. They terrorize villagers. They treat human suffering as raw material for their documentary.

They aren’t interested in understanding the people they’re filming.

They’re interested in getting footage.

And the uglier the footage becomes, the happier they are.

That is the movie’s central idea.

The documentary crew is willing to create suffering because they believe suffering makes good television.

And that’s where Deodato starts turning the knife.

Because the audience is watching the footage for exactly the same reason.

The Found-Footage Trick Was Years Ahead of Its Time

Modern audiences have become accustomed to shaky-camera horror.

made found footage a mainstream phenomenon in 1999. later turned the technique into a major horror franchise.

But was doing something similar in 1980.

And it wasn’t merely using handheld cameras as a stylistic gimmick.

Deodato wanted the footage to look like documentary material.

The compositions are sometimes terrible.

The filmmakers don’t always frame what they’re shooting properly.

The footage looks unfinished.

If the movie had looked like a traditional horror production, the audience could comfortably sit back and say, “It’s just a movie.”

Deodato wanted to remove that safety net.

He wanted viewers to wonder whether the people on screen were actually dying.

Far better than anyone expected.

People Actually Thought It Was Real

The movie’s reputation became so extreme that rumors spread that Deodato had made a genuine snuff film.

The controversy was helped by a marketing strategy that encouraged the idea that the actors had actually disappeared.

The actors had agreed not to appear publicly for a period following the film’s release.

That made the rumors seem plausible.

Then the Italian authorities got involved.

“Mr. Deodato, we’re going to need you to come down to the police station.”

“Because we think you murdered your cast.”

Suddenly your low-budget cannibal movie has become a criminal investigation.

Deodato eventually had to demonstrate that the deaths had been staged and that the supposedly murdered actors were still alive.

The actors appeared in court, proving that the movie hadn’t actually been a snuff film.

But Deodato had created such a convincing illusion that authorities had initially believed otherwise.

That alone would make legendary.

Unfortunately, the reality behind some of the film’s most notorious scenes is much less comfortable.

This is the part where the movie’s “is it real?” controversy becomes genuinely unpleasant.

The human deaths were fake.

The animal deaths weren’t.

Several animals were killed during production and their deaths were filmed.

A turtle was butchered on camera.

Other animals were also killed during production.

The animal scenes weren’t special effects.

They weren’t elaborate makeup effects.

They were real animals being killed for the movie.

That has become one of the most criticized aspects of the production, and understandably so.

Even people who admire as an important piece of horror history have a difficult time defending those sequences.

There’s a major difference between watching a fake human being hacked apart with a special-effects knife and watching an actual animal die.

And that distinction makes some portions of considerably harder to watch today than they were when the movie first became notorious.

The Movie Doesn’t Just Show Violence

This is another reason the movie remains so disturbing.

The violence isn’t simply there because Deodato wanted to see how much blood he could put on screen.

The movie repeatedly uses violence to demonstrate the documentary filmmakers’ moral collapse.

They don’t merely record terrible events.

They interfere with people’s lives.

They manufacture situations.

They behave like people who have discovered that the camera gives them permission to do things they wouldn’t otherwise do.

That makes the filmmakers some of the most unpleasant protagonists in exploitation cinema.

And they’re obsessed with getting footage.

The movie essentially presents them as parasites feeding on human suffering.

The audience is doing the same thing.

And That’s Where Things Get Really Clever

You could argue that is a movie about exploitation made through exploitation.

That’s what makes it so complicated.

Deodato clearly had something to say about sensationalistic media.

He was influenced by the way television news presented real violence to audiences, particularly the disturbing political violence that Italy had experienced.

The movie’s fake documentary crew is basically a group of filmmakers who understand that shocking images sell.

If they can make viewers uncomfortable enough, frightened enough or disgusted enough, they’ll keep watching.

News organizations, television networks and eventually the internet have all learned that disturbing material attracts attention.

The more outrageous the image, the more likely people are to stop scrolling.

Deodato understood this decades before social media turned outrage into a business model.

He was criticizing sensationalism while making one of the most sensationalistic movies imaginable.

That’s either incredibly clever or spectacularly hypocritical.

The Movie’s Most Uncomfortable Question

The most interesting question in isn’t whether the indigenous people are monsters.

It’s whether the filmmakers are.

And then it goes one step further.

Are the filmmakers worse than the people watching them?

That’s a nasty question to ask your audience.

The movie knows exactly what you’re doing.

You’re watching people suffer.

You’re watching because it’s shocking.

You’re waiting for the next horrible thing.

The same impulse drives the fictional documentary crew.

They want the next horrible thing too.

They’re just willing to create it themselves.

The difference between you and them, the movie suggests, is that they have a camera.

That doesn’t exactly make for a comfortable viewing experience.

The “Cannibals” Aren’t Really the Point

The title makes you expect a movie about cannibals.

And sure enough, there are cannibalistic rituals and plenty of gruesome imagery.

But the title is almost a distraction.

The movie’s real subject is exploitation.

The fictional documentary crew arrives expecting to find savages.

Instead, they bring their own brand of savagery with them.

They assume the people they’re filming are primitive.

Meanwhile, the filmmakers themselves behave like violent animals.

The movie deliberately reverses the audience’s expectations.

The “civilized” outsiders become increasingly monstrous.

The supposedly primitive locals become victims of people who believe their cameras make them superior.

It’s a pretty bleak view of humanity.

And it gets bleaker the longer the movie continues.

Then There Is the Sexual Violence

This is where the film moves beyond ordinary gore and into territory that many viewers will simply find intolerable.

annibal Holocaust contains scenes of sexual violence and sexual humiliation.

They’re not presented in the relatively restrained manner that modern mainstream horror might use.

Deodato’s exploitation-film approach means the material is deliberately confrontational.

This is one of the reasons the movie remains difficult to recommend even to people who love extreme horror.

There are movies where you can say, “It’s violent, but it’s fun.”

isn’t really fun.

It wants you to be uncomfortable.

Sometimes it feels like the movie is actively daring you to keep watching.

The Music Makes It Even Stranger

One of the movie’s strangest qualities is the contrast between the horrible images and Riz Ortolani’s score.

The music isn’t constantly screaming at you that something terrible is happening.

Some of it is surprisingly beautiful.

That contrast makes certain sequences even more disturbing.

A beautiful musical passage playing over horrifying images creates a bizarre emotional disconnect.

You’re almost being encouraged to contemplate what you’re seeing rather than simply react to it.

It’s one of the movie’s more effective techniques.

The ugliness isn’t always accompanied by ugly music.

Sometimes it’s accompanied by something hauntingly beautiful.

That makes it feel less like a conventional horror movie and more like a particularly nasty piece of documentary footage.

The Banned-Movie Reputation Made Everything Worse

Once began circulating internationally, its reputation grew.

It became one of the notorious “video nasties” in Britain and was subject to censorship and bans in multiple countries.

And naturally, that made people want to see it even more.

There’s nothing quite like telling horror fans that something is forbidden.

Suddenly everybody needs a copy.

The movie became a forbidden object.

People who had never heard of Ruggero Deodato suddenly knew the title.

People who didn’t even like horror movies wanted to know what could possibly be so bad that governments were trying to stop people from watching it.

The reputation became part of the experience.

And once a movie develops that kind of mythology, it becomes almost impossible to separate the movie itself from the legend surrounding it.

Does It Still Shock Today?

But probably not always for the reasons it shocked audiences in 1980.

Modern audiences have seen much more graphic special effects.

Technology has made it possible to create incredibly realistic digital gore.

We’ve also become accustomed to found footage.

So the basic filmmaking tricks aren’t nearly as revolutionary as they once were.

But still has something many modern extreme horror movies don’t.

There is a nasty atmosphere surrounding the entire production.

You know the controversy.

You know the animals were really killed.

You know the director was accused of making a snuff film.

You know the actors had to prove they weren’t dead.

And then you watch the movie.

That knowledge changes the experience.

You’re not just watching a fictional horror movie.

You’re watching a movie with a history that is almost as bizarre as its fictional story.

One of the Most Messed-Up Movies Ever Made

There are plenty of movies that are more graphically violent than .

There are movies with more gore.

There are movies with more disturbing special effects.

There are movies that are arguably more psychologically horrifying.

But very few movies combine everything that makes so notorious.

You have a fake documentary designed to look real.

You have a director who was investigated because people thought the murders were genuine.

You have actors who were deliberately hidden from the public.

You have genuine animal deaths.

You have extreme violence and sexual violence.

You have a movie about exploitation that is itself deeply exploitative.

You have a film that was banned and censored around the world.

And underneath all of it is a question about why people consume violent images in the first place.

That’s what makes more than just another gore movie.

It’s an uncomfortable experiment.

It wants to make you disgusted.

It wants to make you suspicious.

It wants to make you question the people holding the camera.

And, eventually, it wants you to question yourself for still sitting there watching.

That is a hell of a thing for a horror movie to accomplish.

The strange thing is that isn’t necessarily a movie you’ll enjoy.

Enjoyment almost feels like the wrong measurement.

It’s more like an endurance test.

You wonder what the hell you’re watching.

You remind yourself that the human deaths are fake.

Then you remember that some of the animal deaths aren’t.

You start wondering how the hell this movie was ever released.

Then you realize that somebody deliberately made it this way.

And suddenly the movie becomes even more disturbing.

isn’t the most technically impressive horror movie ever made.

It isn’t the most entertaining.

It certainly isn’t the easiest to recommend.

But when the conversation turns to the most messed-up movies ever made, it belongs near the front of the line.

Not because it has the most blood.

Not because it has the most disgusting special effects.

And not even because it has the most disturbing images.

It belongs there because it crossed the line between movie and reality so effectively that people temporarily forgot they were watching fiction.

And then there’s the truly uncomfortable part:

Some of what they were watching really was real.

That’s the legacy of .

It’s a movie that tried to convince you that you were watching something you shouldn’t be watching.

Forty-plus years later, it still succeeds.

Just maybe not in the way anybody would want.

It’s age restricted obviously so you have to be logged in, but they have it for free on Youtube

items.title: Troma Tuesday: Bloodsucking Freaks
items.author: Schill
items.content:
There are bad movies, there are terrible movies, and then there are movies like , a 1979 exploitation horror film that seems to have been created after someone asked, “What if we took every horrible idea we can think of and put them in one movie?”

Also known as The Incredible Torture Show, the film follows Sardu, the owner of a theater where audiences believe they are watching elaborate stage performances. The problem is that the torture isn’t exactly acting.

Sardu and his assistant Ralphus run a genuinely horrible little business, kidnapping people and subjecting them to increasingly ridiculous forms of torture while wealthy spectators watch and applaud.

So basically, it’s dinner theater for people who should probably be investigated by the police.

The movie wastes almost no time establishing that it has absolutely no interest in good taste. Sardu is played by Seamus O’Brien with the kind of theatrical enthusiasm usually reserved for children’s television villains, except this guy has a torture chamber instead of a magic castle.

His victims are subjected to all sorts of increasingly absurd horrors, and the film presents much of it with a strange combination of exploitation-film sleaze and cheap stage-show comedy.

That’s really the defining characteristic of .

You aren’t supposed to take it seriously.

The production values are extremely low, but that somehow becomes part of the entertainment. Sets look like they were assembled in somebody’s basement, the acting frequently resembles community theater performed by people who have just discovered horror movies, and the special effects range from surprisingly nasty to “someone just threw red paint on that.”

And yet, somehow, it works.

There is a bizarre energy running through the whole thing. The movie constantly seems to be daring the audience to keep watching.

Just when you think you’ve reached the limit, it finds another way to make you wonder why you are still sitting there.

The humor is incredibly dark and frequently offensive, which means this is definitely not a movie that has aged gracefully. A lot of the material is deliberately designed to provoke, and some of it is so tasteless that even exploitation-film veterans may find themselves staring at the screen wondering what exactly they just watched.

But that’s also why the movie developed such a strong cult following.

isn’t trying to be . It isn’t trying to be . It isn’t even particularly interested in being a conventional horror movie.

It’s a midnight-movie experience.

It’s occasionally hilarious.

It’s frequently disgusting.

And every once in a while, you catch yourself laughing at something that probably shouldn’t be funny.

The biggest problem is that the movie’s relentless nastiness can become exhausting. There’s only so much torture, screaming and fake blood a viewer can absorb before the novelty begins to wear off.

Still, if you enjoy bizarre exploitation cinema, is difficult to forget.

It’s less a movie than a dare.

Not remotely respectable.

But if your idea of a good Friday night involves watching a completely unhinged late-1970s exploitation movie and repeatedly asking, “What the hell am I watching?”, delivers exactly what it promises.

items.title: Song Battle: Judas Priest – “Breaking the Law” vs. Iron Maiden – “Run to the Hills”
items.author: Schill
items.content:
Two songs. Two bands. Two completely different approaches to heavy metal.

Judas Priest’s “Breaking the Law” and Iron Maiden’s “Run to the Hills” are among the most recognizable songs in the history of British heavy metal, but they get there in very different ways.

“Breaking the Law” is short, blunt and almost ridiculously simple. It takes one of the greatest metal guitar riffs ever recorded, adds Rob Halford’s unmistakable voice and gets out of the way before it has a chance to overstay its welcome.

“Run to the Hills” is bigger, faster and considerably more ambitious. Bruce Dickinson’s vocals soar over Steve Harris’s galloping bass lines while Dave Murray and Adrian Smith provide the guitars that helped define Iron Maiden’s sound.

One is a compact metal sledgehammer.

The other is a full-speed metal charge.

Both became defining songs for their respective bands. Both helped establish the sound of British heavy metal in the early 1980s.

Song Profile: “Breaking the Law”

Released in 1980 on Judas Priest’s , “Breaking the Law” is one of those songs where the simplicity is the entire point.

The opening guitar riff is immediately recognizable. K.K. Downing and Glenn Tipton don’t need a complicated arrangement to make an impact. The riff is repetitive, muscular and incredibly effective.

Rob Halford’s vocal performance is equally direct. Instead of relying on the high-pitched screams that would become one of his trademarks, Halford delivers the song with a controlled, almost conversational menace.

“Breaking the law” repeated over and over shouldn’t work as well as it does.

The song is barely three minutes long, and there isn’t a second of wasted space. The guitars establish the hook, Halford delivers the attitude, the rhythm section keeps everything moving and the song disappears almost as quickly as it arrived.

That economy is a huge part of its appeal.

Judas Priest didn’t need to demonstrate everything they could do.

They just needed one riff.

Song Profile: “Run to the Hills”

Iron Maiden’s “Run to the Hills” arrived in 1982 on , and it immediately demonstrated how much bigger and more elaborate Maiden’s approach to heavy metal had become.

Steve Harris’s galloping bass line is the engine driving the entire song. The guitars add melodic harmonies and rapid-fire riffs while Clive Burr’s drumming gives the track its relentless momentum.

And then there is Bruce Dickinson.

His vocal performance is one of the song’s defining features. He moves from aggressive verses into soaring, high-energy passages that make the song feel enormous.

“Run to the Hills” also has more structural movement than “Breaking the Law.” It builds, shifts gears and creates the sensation of constantly moving forward.

Where Judas Priest went for maximum impact with minimum ingredients, Iron Maiden packed considerably more musical information into the song.

It is heavier, faster and more technically demanding.

“Breaking the Law” is a masterclass in economy.

The riff is immediately memorable, the structure is easy to follow and the chorus is impossible to forget.

But “Run to the Hills” is considerably more ambitious. The arrangement moves between contrasting sections while maintaining a strong central hook. Harris builds the song around that galloping rhythm and gives the guitars plenty of room to add melodic detail.

“Breaking the Law” is incredibly efficient.

“Run to the Hills” is more developed.

Priest gets maximum results from minimal ingredients, but Maiden’s songwriting is more sophisticated.

This is a battle between two of heavy metal’s greatest singers.

Rob Halford’s performance on “Breaking the Law” is remarkably restrained. He doesn’t need to scream his way through the song. His delivery gives the track an attitude that makes the lyrics feel almost casually rebellious.

Bruce Dickinson takes the opposite approach.

His performance on “Run to the Hills” is explosive. The high notes, aggression and sheer range make the vocal one of the song’s most memorable elements.

Dickinson is spectacular.

Dickinson’s performance gives Maiden the edge.

This may be the closest round of the entire battle.

“Breaking the Law” has one of the most recognizable guitar riffs in metal history. You don’t need the drums, bass or vocals. Give someone the riff and they immediately know the song.

“Run to the Hills” has several excellent guitar parts, including its famous galloping passages and harmonized sections.

But this isn’t really close.

The Priest riff is one of those riffs that has escaped the boundaries of heavy metal and become part of popular culture.

Judas Priest takes this round easily.

Round 4: Bass & Rhythm Section

“Breaking the Law” has a tight, straightforward rhythm section that serves the guitar riff perfectly.

But Iron Maiden has Steve Harris.

Harris’s bass isn’t simply sitting underneath the guitars. It drives “Run to the Hills.” That galloping bass style became one of the defining characteristics of Iron Maiden’s sound.

Clive Burr matches him with rapid, energetic drumming that keeps the entire track moving at a furious pace.

Maiden’s rhythm section is doing considerably more work.

“Breaking the Law” is energetic, but its power comes from its stomp.

It feels like a fist coming straight at you.

“Run to the Hills” feels like being chased by that fist.

The galloping rhythm creates constant forward momentum, and the drums and guitars make the song feel like it is accelerating even when the tempo itself remains controlled.

The Maiden track simply has more velocity.

For sheer adrenaline, Iron Maiden takes it.

This is another round where simplicity wins.

“Breaking the law” is one of those choruses that requires absolutely no explanation. Even someone who has never heard the entire song probably knows what comes next once the riff starts.

“Run to the Hills” has a fantastic chorus, but it is more dependent on Dickinson’s vocal performance and the surrounding arrangement.

The Priest chorus is practically a chant.

And it sticks in your head immediately.

Judas Priest wins on pure memorability.

“British Steel” has a relatively stripped-down production compared with the increasingly elaborate metal records that followed it.

That works perfectly for “Breaking the Law.” Everything is clear, punchy and focused around the riff.

gives “Run to the Hills” a much bigger sound. The guitars have more dimension, the drums hit harder and Dickinson’s vocals dominate the track.

The Maiden production makes the song feel enormous.

The larger production suits Maiden’s bigger musical approach.

Both songs helped define their bands.

“Breaking the Law” took heavy metal’s basic ingredients and stripped them down to an almost punk-like simplicity. It proved that metal didn’t always need lengthy guitar solos or complicated arrangements to be effective.

“Run to the Hills” helped establish another side of the genre: melodic, ambitious and technically demanding heavy metal.

Iron Maiden’s approach was more distinctive.

The galloping bass, harmonized guitars and Dickinson’s vocals created a sound that was unmistakably Maiden.

Maiden gets the edge for creating a more distinctive musical identity within the song.

“Breaking the Law” is one of the songs that immediately comes to mind when people think of classic heavy metal.

The music video became famous for its ridiculous bank robbery storyline, while the song itself became a permanent part of Judas Priest’s live repertoire.

But “Run to the Hills” had an enormous impact too.

It became one of Iron Maiden’s signature songs and helped make one of the landmark albums of the New Wave of British Heavy Metal.

Both songs became gateways into metal for generations of listeners.

But Priest’s song has one advantage.

You don’t even have to be a metal fan to recognize it.

The riff and chorus have become almost universally recognizable.

Round 10: Overall Metal Factor

This is where the battle gets interesting.

“Breaking the Law” represents one of metal’s greatest strengths: simplicity.

It’s loud, aggressive, memorable and impossible to mistake for anything else.

“Run to the Hills” represents another side of metal: speed, musicianship, melodic guitar work, powerful vocals and a sense of scale.

If “Breaking the Law” is the guy standing in the parking lot with a leather jacket and a guitar riff, “Run to the Hills” is the guy charging over the hill on horseback with an entire army behind him.

But if we’re judging which song packs more of the genre’s defining characteristics into one track, Maiden has the advantage.

Iron Maiden takes the final round.

Breaking the Law — 4 rounds

Run to the Hills — 6 rounds

The Winner: “Run to the Hills”

Iron Maiden takes the battle, but Judas Priest absolutely makes them work for it.

“Breaking the Law” might actually be the more instantly recognizable song. Its guitar riff is legendary, its chorus is ridiculously catchy and its short running time makes it almost impossible to get tired of.

But “Run to the Hills” does more.

The songwriting is more ambitious. The rhythm section is more dynamic. The vocals are more demanding. The guitars are more elaborate. And the entire performance feels like it is operating at maximum speed.

Judas Priest perfected the metal .

Iron Maiden perfected the metal .

“Breaking the Law” is the song you hear once and immediately remember.

“Run to the Hills” is the song that makes you want to turn the volume up.

And when these two giants go head-to-head, that extra musical firepower gives Iron Maiden the victory.

Winner: Iron Maiden — “Run to the Hills”

items.title: Saturday 80s Jam: Flashdance…What a Feeling – Irene Cara
items.author: Schill
items.content:
Few songs capture the sheer optimism of the early 1980s quite like Irene Cara’s “Flashdance… What a Feeling.” It is a song about ambition, determination, dreams, and the almost ridiculous confidence that everything might actually work out if you just believe in yourself hard enough.

Released in 1983 as the centerpiece of the soundtrack to , the song became much bigger than the movie. It was a massive international hit, a defining song of its era, and one of the most recognizable combinations of pop music and cinema ever recorded.

It also represented a remarkable moment in Irene Cara’s career. Only a few years earlier, she had already become famous for “Fame,” the title song from the 1980 film and television series. “Flashdance… What a Feeling” turned her into one of the biggest pop stars in the world.

The song’s success wasn’t accidental. It was the product of an unusually effective combination of musicians, writers, producers, technology, and a movie perfectly suited to the cultural moment.

And at the center of all of it was Cara’s voice.

Irene Cara was already an established star before “Flashdance… What a Feeling.”

Born in New York City, Cara began performing as a child and built an impressive résumé in theater, television, and music. Her major breakthrough came with , the 1980 film about students at New York’s High School of Performing Arts.

Cara played Coco Hernandez, one of the film’s central characters, and performed the title song.

“Fame” became an enormous hit.

The song won the Academy Award for Best Original Song and helped establish Cara as an artist capable of crossing between acting and music without either career feeling like a side project.

That distinction became important when arrived.

The movie’s central character, Alex Owens, is a young woman working as a welder while pursuing her dream of becoming a professional dancer.

It was essentially the perfect setup for a big inspirational pop song.

The challenge was creating one that didn’t feel like generic movie soundtrack filler.

The solution came from a remarkable songwriting collaboration.

Giorgio Moroder Enters the Picture

The music for “Flashdance… What a Feeling” was written by Giorgio Moroder, Keith Forsey, and Irene Cara.

Moroder was already one of the most important figures in electronic pop music.

The Italian-born producer had helped pioneer the use of synthesizers, drum machines, sequencers, and electronic production techniques in mainstream music.

His work with Donna Summer had already transformed dance music.

By the early 1980s, electronic instruments were becoming increasingly important to pop music, and Moroder understood how to combine those sounds with traditional songwriting.

Keith Forsey was another crucial part of the equation.

A highly experienced musician and producer, Forsey had worked on numerous recordings and was deeply involved with the emerging sound of 1980s pop.

Cara herself contributed to the lyrics.

That combination gave the song something particularly effective: it sounded futuristic without abandoning the emotional directness of a traditional pop song.

The synthesizers made it sound like 1983.

Cara’s vocal made it feel timeless.

was released in April 1983.

The movie itself was not initially expected to become a phenomenon on the scale it eventually did.

Its story was relatively straightforward.

Alex Owens works a physically demanding job during the day while dancing at night. She dreams of being accepted into a prestigious dance school but struggles with confidence, money, and the circumstances of her life.

It is classic underdog storytelling.

But had something else working in its favor.

The movie was built around movement, music, lighting, editing, and visual style.

The famous dance sequences became enormously influential.

And the soundtrack was essential to the movie’s identity.

Instead of treating the music as something happening behind the story, essentially made the music part of the story.

That was a major reason the soundtrack became such a phenomenon.

And “Flashdance… What a Feeling” was its emotional centerpiece.

The song begins with a sound that immediately places you in the early 1980s.

The synthesizer arrangement creates an atmosphere that feels almost cinematic before Cara sings a word.

She doesn’t ease into the performance.

She sounds completely committed.

That is one of the song’s greatest strengths.

There is no ironic distance.

No attempt to make the sentiment seem cooler than it is.

“Flashdance… What a Feeling” believes in its message completely.

That kind of sincerity can be difficult to pull off.

In lesser hands, an inspirational song can become unbearably cheesy.

She sounds like someone who genuinely believes that ambition and hard work can change a person’s life.

That conviction is what makes the song work.

The chorus is the part everybody knows.

It rises dramatically, building from the verses into a huge, soaring declaration.

The melody is simple enough to remember instantly but powerful enough to create a sense of release.

That combination is extremely difficult to achieve.

The best pop choruses feel inevitable.

Once you hear the verses, you can almost sense where the song needs to go.

“Flashdance… What a Feeling” does exactly that.

The production keeps increasing the scale until the chorus feels enormous.

The rhythm becomes more forceful.

Cara pushes her voice higher.

Everything is designed to create momentum.

And then the song gives you exactly what you were waiting for.

The song’s greatest trick may be the way it connects physical movement with emotional ambition.

The lyrics describe the sensation of dancing and the feeling of pursuing a dream, but the song itself also behaves like a dance.

The rhythm is steady and propulsive.

The synthesizers provide constant forward movement.

The arrangement builds rather than simply repeating.

It feels like something is happening.

That made it particularly effective in , where dance itself represents freedom and self-expression.

Alex isn’t simply trying to become a better dancer.

She is trying to become a different version of herself.

The song gives that transformation a musical voice.

Listening to “Flashdance… What a Feeling” today is also an interesting lesson in how quickly pop production can define an era.

The synthesizers are unmistakably early 1980s.

The drum sounds are enormous.

The production has a polished, electronic sheen that would have been difficult to achieve in the same way a decade earlier.

This was the era when electronic instruments were moving from experimental studios into mainstream pop.

Artists were discovering that technology didn’t have to replace emotion.

Moroder understood that particularly well.

His productions could be mechanical without feeling cold.

The technology created the architecture.

The human voice provided the emotion.

That balance became one of the defining sounds of 1980s pop.

“Flashdance… What a Feeling” became one of the biggest singles of 1983.

It reached number one on the Billboard Hot 100 in the United States and topped charts in numerous other countries.

The song became a fixture on radio stations, MTV, movie soundtracks, television programs, dance floors, and eventually countless compilations celebrating the music of the 1980s.

Its success also helped turn the soundtrack into a major commercial success.

The movie and soundtrack effectively fed each other.

People watched the movie and wanted the music.

People heard the music and wanted to see the movie.

That relationship between cinema and pop music would become increasingly important throughout the decade.

The song’s success reached another level at the 1984 Academy Awards.

“Flashdance… What a Feeling” won the Academy Award for Best Original Song.

For Irene Cara, it was another Oscar-winning song following “Fame.”

That made her a rare artist to become closely associated with multiple Academy Award-winning movie songs.

The achievement was even more impressive because Cara wasn’t simply the performer.

She was also one of the song’s lyricists.

Her involvement gave the song a personal connection to the character and story rather than making her merely the voice hired to sing someone else’s composition.

The Song Became Bigger Than the Movie

One of the most interesting things about “Flashdance… What a Feeling” is that you don’t need to have seen to know it.

That isn’t true of every successful movie song.

Some become inseparable from a particular scene.

Others are remembered primarily because of the movie.

“Flashdance… What a Feeling” escaped that limitation.

It became a standalone pop song.

You could hear it on the radio without knowing anything about Alex Owens.

The message worked independently.

That is one reason the song has survived.

Its subject isn’t really dancing.

It is the idea of wanting something badly enough to pursue it.

That is considerably more universal.

The song also arrived at exactly the right moment for MTV.

Music television was transforming the relationship between artists and audiences.

A successful song could now become a visual experience as well as an audio one.

“Flashdance… What a Feeling” benefited enormously from that environment.

The imagery associated with became part of the song’s identity.

The entire visual vocabulary of the movie became intertwined with the song.

It is difficult to hear the opening synthesizer today without immediately imagining the visual world of .

That is the power of a great soundtrack song.

The biggest question with many 1980s hits is whether they survive once the production style becomes dated.

Synthesizers can sound dated.

Drum machines can sound dated.

Fashion certainly becomes dated.

But “Flashdance… What a Feeling” continues to work because its emotional core is stronger than its production technology.

The technology gives it historical character.

Cara’s performance gives it longevity.

There is an almost startling lack of cynicism in the song.

It isn’t trying to convince you that dreams are stupid.

It isn’t telling you that success is guaranteed.

It simply embraces the idea that pursuing something you love can be exhilarating.

That message has an enormous amount of staying power.

Cara’s voice is perhaps the most important ingredient.

She had tremendous control, but she never made the performance feel overly technical.

The song requires power without screaming.

Emotion without melodrama.

Confidence without arrogance.

Her voice gets larger as the song progresses, but the performance never loses its musicality.

That is why countless singers have performed the song over the years without necessarily capturing the magic of the original.

The melody is accessible.

It is much harder to reproduce the feeling.

“Flashdance… What a Feeling” became one of the defining songs of the 1980s.

Its influence can be heard indirectly in countless inspirational pop songs that followed.

The formula became familiar:

Start with a personal dream.

Introduce a massive chorus.

Make the production enormous.

End with the listener feeling like they can accomplish something.

But what makes the original special is that it doesn’t feel like a formula when you’re hearing it.

It feels like a genuine emotional release.

That is partly because the song arrived before the formula had become overused.

And partly because Irene Cara was exceptionally good at selling it.

More Than a Nostalgia Song

It would be easy to dismiss “Flashdance… What a Feeling” as simply another nostalgic 1980s hit.

That would miss what made it important.

Yes, the synthesizers scream 1983.

Yes, the song is associated with leg warmers, dance movies, neon colors, and the visual culture of the decade.

But underneath all of that is a remarkably efficient piece of pop songwriting.

And the connection to the movie works.

Every component is doing the same thing.

Everything points upward.

That is why the song feels so uplifting.

It was constructed to create momentum from beginning to end.

Irene Cara’s Complicated Legacy

Cara’s career after “Flashdance… What a Feeling” never reached the same level of mainstream dominance.

That can sometimes cause an artist’s legacy to become distorted.

People remember the song but forget the performer.

They remember the movie but forget the person whose voice made the song unforgettable.

That is unfortunate because Cara had already demonstrated her abilities years earlier with “Fame.”

Together, “Fame” and “Flashdance… What a Feeling” represent two of the defining movie songs of the early 1980s.

They also demonstrate how important Cara was to the sound of that period.

She wasn’t simply lucky enough to sing two successful songs.

She had the voice and performance ability necessary to turn them into cultural landmarks.

A Song That Refuses to Quit

The best inspirational songs can sometimes become irritating because they try too hard to inspire.

“Flashdance… What a Feeling” avoids that problem because it sounds joyous rather than preachy.

It doesn’t feel like somebody giving you a motivational speech.

It feels like somebody discovering something.

The excitement is contagious.

That’s why the song continues to appear in movies, television programs, commercials, sporting events, karaoke rooms, dance performances, and countless 1980s retrospectives.

People recognize it almost instantly.

The opening notes arrive, and you know exactly where you’re going.

For a few minutes, everything becomes bigger.

The dream seems possible.

And Irene Cara sounds absolutely convinced that something wonderful is about to happen.

“Flashdance… What a Feeling” is one of those rare songs where the movie, the singer, the songwriting, and the production all became inseparable.

Giorgio Moroder and Keith Forsey provided the musical framework.

Irene Cara helped shape the words and delivered the definitive performance.

provided the story.

The early 1980s provided the technological and cultural moment.

Together, they created something that has lasted far longer than anyone could reasonably have expected from a song written for a dance movie.

The production may immediately transport you back to 1983.

The synthesizers may sound like 1983.

The fashion associated with it may scream 1983.

But the emotion doesn’t belong to any particular decade.

Wanting to achieve something.

Feeling terrified that you might fail.

And then, for one glorious moment, believing that you actually can do it.

That’s what “Flashdance… What a Feeling” captured.

And Irene Cara made us believe it.
