items.title: Forgotten Band: The Damned
items.author: Schill
items.content:
There is a strange little corner of rock history occupied by bands that were important enough to change music but somehow never became household names. The Damned sit comfortably in that category.

If you know punk, you know The Damned. If you know British rock history, you probably know The Damned. If you have ever gone down a rabbit hole involving punk, goth, post-punk, garage rock, or alternative music, you’ve almost certainly encountered them.

But ask the average person to name the most important British punk bands and you’re likely to hear the Sex Pistols, The Clash, and perhaps The Buzzcocks. The Damned might eventually appear somewhere down the list.

That is remarkable because The Damned were there from the very beginning.

They were not merely observers of the original British punk explosion. They were one of the bands responsible for creating it.

They were the first British punk band to release a single. They released one of the first British punk albums. They played fast, loud, obnoxious music before most of the country had even figured out what punk was supposed to sound like.

And then, rather than spending the rest of their career making the same record over and over, they started changing.

They became darker. Stranger. More theatrical. More melodic. More psychedelic. More gothic. At various points they sounded like a punk band, a garage band, a goth band, a psychedelic rock group, and a completely unhinged rock ‘n’ roll circus.

That refusal to stay in one box may have been part of the reason they never became as commercially recognizable as some of their contemporaries.

It is also exactly what makes The Damned so interesting.

The Damned emerged in London during the mid-1970s, when the British music scene was beginning to fracture.

Progressive rock had become increasingly elaborate. Arena rock was getting bigger and more polished. Glam had provided an explosion of theatricality, but even that movement was becoming part of the established music business.

Meanwhile, a collection of young musicians were discovering that you didn’t need enormous budgets, virtuoso musicianship, or twenty-minute songs to make something exciting.

The original Damned lineup featured Dave Vanian on vocals, Captain Sensible on guitar, Rat Scabies on drums, and Brian James on guitar. It was an unlikely combination of personalities, but together they created something that was immediate and confrontational.

Dave Vanian looked like he had wandered out of a horror movie.

Captain Sensible looked like he might have wandered in from an entirely different one.

And the music sounded like somebody had plugged a jet engine into a Marshall amplifier.

The Damned were not interested in sounding respectable.

New Rose Changes Everything

In October 1976, The Damned released “New Rose.”

It is difficult to overstate the historical importance of that record.

“New Rose” is widely recognized as the first single released by a British punk band.

The Sex Pistols were generating enormous controversy. The Clash were beginning to develop their identity. The Buzzcocks were emerging from Manchester.

But The Damned got their record out first.

And they didn’t ease anybody into the new musical landscape.

“New Rose” was short, aggressive, fast, and completely uninterested in traditional rock-radio conventions.

It sounded like a band trying to kick down the door.

The single immediately established something that would become a recurring theme throughout The Damned’s career: they were capable of being ridiculous and dangerous at exactly the same time.

There was humor underneath the aggression.

There was theatricality underneath the speed.

And there was a genuine love of old-fashioned rock ‘n’ roll underneath all the noise.

That combination would become one of their defining characteristics.

In February 1977, The Damned released .

The album was produced by Nick Lowe and became one of the foundational records of British punk.

It was also incredibly short.

The entire thing moves like somebody has just announced that the building is on fire.

There isn’t much interest in wasting time.

Songs arrive, explode, and disappear before you’ve had time to get comfortable.

The album contains some of the band’s best-known early material, including “Neat Neat Neat” and “New Rose,” but what makes the record important is its sense of urgency.

The Damned weren’t trying to construct elaborate arrangements.

They weren’t interested in proving how technically sophisticated they were.

They wanted the songs to hit.

The album helped establish the template for British punk’s first wave: short songs, loud guitars, furious drumming, memorable hooks, and an attitude that suggested the entire music industry could probably survive without them.

The irony is that the music industry eventually couldn’t ignore them.

The Band That Wouldn’t Behave

The Damned quickly developed a reputation for chaos.

That reputation wasn’t entirely accidental.

Captain Sensible was one of the more colorful personalities in British punk. Dave Vanian brought a theatrical, almost gothic presence to the band. Rat Scabies was a ferocious drummer. Brian James brought a darker, more traditional punk-rock guitar sound.

They didn’t necessarily look like a conventional rock band.

They didn’t act like one either.

And they certainly didn’t sound like one for very long.

After their first album, Brian James departed following internal tensions and disagreements.

Instead of collapsing, The Damned began moving in a completely different direction.

This is where their story gets particularly interesting.

Most punk bands faced a basic choice: continue making increasingly polished versions of their original sound or evolve into something else.

The Damned chose option three.

They seemed determined to see how many different musical identities they could cram into one career.

The band’s second album, , arrived in 1977.

It was not received as enthusiastically as the debut.

Part of the problem was that it was already showing signs that The Damned weren’t interested in simply repeating themselves.

Captain Sensible was increasingly involved in the band’s musical direction, and their sound was becoming more experimental.

The Damned eventually broke up.

For most bands, that would have been the end.

For The Damned, it was more like an intermission.

They returned in the late 1970s with a different sound and a significantly different atmosphere.

The punk fury was still there, but it was being replaced by something more sinister.

Something more atmospheric.

Something that would help lay groundwork for gothic rock.

Then came in 1979.

This is where the argument for The Damned’s importance becomes almost impossible to ignore.

The album contains punk, garage rock, psychedelic influences, pop hooks, and the beginnings of the darker sound that would become associated with goth.

“Love Song” showed that The Damned could write something catchy without losing their edge.

“Smash It Up” demonstrated their ability to turn punk aggression into something almost celebratory.

And “Plan 9 Channel 7” leaned heavily into the band’s fascination with horror, atmosphere, and 1960s garage rock.

The Damned were becoming something much bigger than a punk band.

They were becoming a strange hybrid of everything they liked.

That was one of their greatest strengths.

They weren’t embarrassed to love pop music.

They weren’t embarrassed to love horror movies.

They weren’t embarrassed to love psychedelic rock.

They weren’t embarrassed to love garage rock.

And they certainly weren’t embarrassed to make fun of themselves.

If The Damned are remembered for anything beyond punk, it is their influence on gothic rock.

Dave Vanian’s appearance had already given the band a visual identity unlike most of their punk contemporaries.

With his pale makeup, dark clothing, and theatrical presentation, Vanian looked less like a punk singer and more like a rock-and-roll vampire.

And then there was the music.

The band’s next major phase would push further into dark, atmospheric territory.

, released in 1980, demonstrated just how far they had traveled from the frantic three-chord assault of .

The album included lengthy, atmospheric material alongside more conventional songs.

It wasn’t simply punk anymore.

The Damned were becoming one of those bands where the label started getting in the way.

Calling them punk was accurate.

Calling them goth was also reasonable.

Calling them rock was obvious.

Calling them weird was probably the most accurate description of all.

“Eloise” and the Commercial Peak

The Damned’s career took another unexpected turn in the mid-1980s.

They scored one of their biggest commercial successes with their cover of “Eloise.”

The song was dramatically different from the stripped-down punk of their early years.

The arrangement was theatrical and bombastic, while Vanian’s voice gave the song an appropriately dramatic quality.

The single became a major British hit and demonstrated that The Damned could operate within a much larger musical world than the punk scene that had originally produced them.

But by then the band’s history had become a revolving door of personnel changes, breakups, reunions, and different musical directions.

Captain Sensible had departed for a successful solo career.

Vanian remained the central figure.

And The Damned continued.

That word may be the most important one in their entire story.

The Captain Sensible Problem

One reason The Damned’s history can be difficult for casual listeners to follow is that Captain Sensible became successful outside the band.

His solo career produced the massive novelty hit “Happy Talk” in 1982, which reached number one in the United Kingdom.

That song could hardly have been further removed from the image of The Damned.

This was the same Captain Sensible who had helped create some of the most aggressive British punk music of the 1970s.

Suddenly he was wearing a giant red beret and appearing on mainstream television.

It was also completely consistent with his personality.

Captain Sensible had never seemed particularly interested in following the rules of what a punk musician was supposed to be.

The success of his solo career also contributed to the increasingly unusual trajectory of The Damned.

They were no longer simply one band following one musical path.

They were a collection of personalities constantly pulling the group in different directions.

Somehow, they kept coming back together.

Why Didn’t They Become as Famous as The Clash?

This is the question that hangs over The Damned.

Why aren’t they generally mentioned alongside The Clash and the Sex Pistols when discussing the defining British punk bands?

There isn’t one simple answer.

The Sex Pistols became cultural lightning rods.

The Clash developed into one of the most politically significant rock bands of their era.

The Damned were different.

They didn’t have a single ideological message that defined them.

They didn’t build their identity around political confrontation.

They didn’t become the voice of a particular movement.

They were more interested in music itself.

They were also inconsistent in a way that made them fascinating but perhaps harder to market.

A listener could discover The Damned through punk, goth, garage rock, alternative music, or even mainstream British pop.

The band’s catalog didn’t have one obvious identity.

And commercially, they never maintained the sustained success required to become one of the biggest bands of their generation.

But that doesn’t mean they weren’t influential.

In fact, their influence may be easier to hear in other bands than in their own record sales.

The Forgotten Link Between Punk and Goth

The Damned occupy a fascinating position in British music.

They were part of the original punk explosion, but their willingness to experiment helped point toward the darker alternative music that followed.

That makes them an important bridge between several movements.

You can hear elements of punk’s speed and aggression.

You can hear garage rock.

You can hear psychedelic rock.

You can hear horror-film imagery.

You can hear the beginnings of gothic rock.

You can hear pop songwriting.

You can even hear the seeds of the alternative rock that would become much more prominent in the 1980s and 1990s.

They weren’t necessarily inventing each of those things independently.

Their importance comes from combining them.

The Damned essentially treated genres as suggestions rather than rules.

A Band That Refused to Grow Up

There is also something wonderfully strange about The Damned’s longevity.

Many punk bands eventually became serious.

The Damned never entirely did.

It may have been their secret weapon.

There was always a sense that they understood rock music was supposed to be fun.

Even when the music became darker, there was still humor underneath it.

Even when the band became more theatrical, there was still punk aggression.

Even when they experimented, they never completely abandoned the simple pleasure of turning up the volume and making a lot of noise.

That attitude allowed them to survive changes in musical fashion that destroyed plenty of other bands.

Post-punk became new wave.

New wave became goth and alternative rock.

The 1980s became the 1990s.

Alternative rock became mainstream.

And The Damned were still around.

The easiest way to understand The Damned’s legacy is to stop looking for one particular sound.

They weren’t important because they created a single genre.

They were important because they demonstrated how much freedom a rock band could have.

A band could be punk and melodic.

It could be aggressive and funny.

It could be dark without taking itself too seriously.

It could move from two-minute punk songs to extended psychedelic pieces.

It could wear horror-movie imagery without becoming a novelty act.

And it could change without completely losing its identity.

That is a difficult trick.

Most bands that change dramatically eventually sound like different bands.

The Damned often sounded like The Damned even when the music around them was completely different.

So, Are The Damned Really Forgotten?

Among punk fans, they are anything but forgotten.

Among musicians, their influence is obvious.

Among people who know British alternative music, their name carries considerable weight.

But compared with the fame of The Clash, the Sex Pistols, or even later bands influenced by them, The Damned remain strangely underappreciated by the wider public.

And perhaps that is the great irony of their career.

They were one of the first British punk bands to put a record on the shelves.

They released one of the most important early punk albums.

They helped establish the sound and attitude of British punk.

They helped point toward gothic rock.

They produced some genuinely great rock songs.

They survived numerous personnel changes and breakups.

They continued recording and performing decades after the original punk explosion.

And yet they somehow remain the band people discover after they have already discovered everybody else.

Maybe that is actually the best way to discover The Damned.

Start with the obvious names.

Listen to the Sex Pistols.

Then eventually someone mentions The Damned.

You put on expecting another historical punk artifact.

Instead, you discover a band that sounds alive.

Then you hear and realize they’re doing something completely different.

Then you hear .

Then you find the gothic material.

Then Captain Sensible’s solo work.

Suddenly the supposedly “forgotten” band has turned into a rabbit hole.

And that’s probably the most appropriate fate for The Damned.

They were never particularly good at staying where people expected them to stay.

Why should their place in rock history be any different?

The Damned weren’t simply one of the first British punk bands.

They were one of the bands that proved punk could become almost anything.

The fact that they never became as famous as some of their contemporaries doesn’t make their story less important.

If anything, it makes rediscovering them more rewarding.

The Damned weren’t forgotten because they weren’t important.

They were forgotten because rock history has a bad habit of simplifying itself.

Punk becomes three bands.

Goth becomes another handful.

Alternative rock gets its own list.

Garage rock gets another.

The messy connections between all of them disappear.

The Damned don’t fit neatly into any of those boxes.

They belong in all of them.

And that’s exactly why, more than four decades after their debut, The Damned still sound like a band waiting to be rediscovered.

items.title: Hump Day Hottie: Leni Klum
items.author: Schill
items.content:
Leni Klum is a German-American model who has developed her own career in fashion while growing up in the public eye. Born May 4, 2004, in New York City, she is the daughter of supermodel and television personality Heidi Klum and Italian businessman Flavio Briatore. Leni was raised primarily by her mother and stepfather, musician Seal, and later began pursuing modeling professionally.

She made her modeling debut alongside Heidi Klum in a 2020 cover and fashion editorial for Vogue Germany, quickly attracting attention as the daughter of one of the fashion industry’s most recognizable figures. Since then, Leni has appeared in campaigns and editorials for major fashion and beauty brands and has walked in runway shows. Her work has included appearances for Dolce & Gabbana and other prominent designers.

While her family background has naturally generated media interest, Leni has increasingly established herself as a model in her own right. With her distinctive look, growing fashion portfolio, and international exposure, she represents a new generation of celebrity-connected models.

items.title: Troma Tuesday: Stuck on You!
items.author: Schill
items.content:
Before Troma became famous for toxic waste, mutant superheroes and outrageous splatter, the company spent several years making something considerably different: raunchy comedies. is one of the strangest examples of that early period, taking the familiar problem of a couple having relationship difficulties and turning it into a bizarre trip through the entire history of romance.

Directed by Lloyd Kaufman and Michael Herz, was released in the early 1980s and runs approximately 88 minutes. The movie stars Professor Irwin Corey as Judge Gabriel, with Virginia Penta and Mark Mikulski playing the troubled couple at the center of the story.

It’s part romantic comedy, part sketch comedy, part historical parody and part sex comedy. In typical Troma fashion, it doesn’t seem particularly interested in worrying about whether those ingredients actually belong together.

Bill and Carol Have Problems

Bill Andrews and Carol Griffiths are in love.

Unfortunately, they’re also having problems.

Their relationship has deteriorated to the point where they’ve ended up in Family Court, where they meet Judge Gabriel. Played by the legendary comedian Irwin Corey, Gabriel is unlike any ordinary judge.

Instead of simply listening to the couple’s arguments and making a ruling, he decides that Bill and Carol need a history lesson.

His solution is to take them on a bizarre journey through time.

The judge shows them couples from different periods of history, demonstrating that the problems they’re experiencing aren’t exactly new.

Apparently, romantic arguments have been around for a very long time.

This is where really becomes its own peculiar thing.

The movie jumps through various historical periods and reimagines famous couples and events through the lens of Troma-style comedy.

Among the figures who appear are Adam and Eve, Christopher Columbus and Queen Isabella, Napoleon, King Arthur and Guinevere, and other famous historical characters.

Instead of presenting history with any concern for accuracy, the filmmakers use these characters as launching pads for jokes.

The basic message is simple: people have been screwing up relationships forever.

The historical figures change.

The relationship problems remain remarkably familiar.

Adam and Eve Get the Troma Treatment

The Adam and Eve sequence immediately establishes the movie’s attitude toward history.

Rather than treating the biblical story with solemnity, turns it into a bawdy comedy sketch.

That’s essentially the formula for the entire movie.

Historical events become setups.

Famous people become punchlines.

Romance becomes an excuse for increasingly ridiculous situations.

The filmmakers clearly weren’t attempting to make a serious historical parody. Their targets were broad, their humor was deliberately juvenile, and the whole thing was designed to keep moving from one outrageous bit to another.

From Columbus to King Arthur

The movie’s historical journey continues with Christopher Columbus and Queen Isabella before eventually moving into other periods.

One of the funniest aspects of the concept is how casually the movie throws famous historical figures into the same universe.

Christopher Columbus becomes part of a sex joke.

Napoleon becomes part of a relationship joke.

King Arthur and Guinevere become part of another romantic farce.

It’s basically history class taught by people who would rather make dirty jokes than explain anything.

The result isn’t sophisticated satire.

It’s closer to an extended series of comedy sketches connected by Bill and Carol’s relationship.

Irwin Corey Steals the Show

The secret weapon is Irwin Corey.

Corey was a veteran comedian known for his eccentric, deliberately nonsensical style. His performance as Judge Gabriel gives the movie much of its personality.

He plays the judge with an exaggerated seriousness that makes the increasingly ridiculous situations even funnier.

Corey doesn’t have to behave like everyone else.

He can stand there delivering bizarre pronouncements while the rest of the cast reacts to him.

That contrast works particularly well because the movie itself is constantly shifting between relatively normal relationship scenes and complete nonsense.

Judge Gabriel is essentially the tour guide through all of it.

The Surprise Behind Judge Gabriel

The movie eventually reveals that Judge Gabriel isn’t simply a strange family-court judge.

There’s a supernatural reason for his unusual abilities.

That revelation gives the entire story another layer and explains why he can take Bill and Carol on their bizarre journey through history.

It also reinforces the movie’s central idea.

Their relationship problems aren’t unique.

They are part of something that has existed for as long as humans have been falling in love, fighting, making up and making the same mistakes all over again.

The message is actually fairly sweet underneath all the crude humor.

Unfortunately, Troma isn’t exactly the company you’d expect to deliver that message with subtlety.

Troma Before The Toxic Avenger

For modern audiences, the most interesting thing about may be its place in Troma history.

The film belongs to the company’s early run of “sexy comedies,” which included , and .

These movies helped establish Troma before the company became internationally associated with .

That makes an interesting time capsule.

The Troma style is already there, but the ingredients are different.

Instead of radioactive waste and monsters, the filmmakers are working with sex, historical parody, slapstick and deliberately cheap-looking comedy.

It’s basically Troma figuring out what kind of crazy movie it wants to become.

The filmmakers have described as a tribute to comedy influences including Mel Brooks, Tom Lehrer and Stan Freberg.

That influence is easy to understand.

The movie treats historical figures as toys.

It takes familiar stories and twists them into comedy.

It isn’t interested in maintaining the dignity of famous people.

That’s very much in the tradition of historical parody.

The difference is that Mel Brooks had considerably more money, resources and filmmaking polish.

And enthusiasm can only take you so far.

The limitations of the production are obvious.

The sets are inexpensive.

The costumes aren’t exactly designed to fool historians.

The jokes are hit-or-miss.

Some sequences feel like sketches that were stretched into feature length.

But there’s an undeniable charm to the whole thing.

feels handmade.

It has the energy of a group of filmmakers who simply wanted to make something funny and outrageous without worrying too much about conventional standards.

That approach would eventually become one of Troma’s defining characteristics.

That’s going to depend heavily on your tolerance for early-1980s raunchy comedy.

Others are painfully dated.

The movie’s humor is broad, sexual and frequently juvenile.

There’s very little subtlety.

But there are also genuinely clever ideas buried inside the silliness, particularly the decision to use history as a way of showing that relationship problems are timeless.

The movie’s biggest weakness is that it sometimes feels like a collection of unrelated comedy bits rather than a fully developed story.

Then again, that’s also part of its charm.

You’re never quite sure what ridiculous historical scenario is coming next.

The Legacy of Stuck on You!

isn’t one of Troma’s best-known movies, and it has been overshadowed by the much more famous films that followed it.

But for anyone interested in the company’s history, it’s an entertaining curiosity.

It shows Troma before the company had fully established the outrageous horror identity that would make it famous.

It also demonstrates that Lloyd Kaufman and Michael Herz were willing to experiment with different kinds of low-budget comedy.

The movie may not have aged perfectly, but it remains a fascinating snapshot of independent filmmaking in the early 1980s.

Ultimately, has a surprisingly simple idea beneath all the jokes.

Relationships are complicated.

People have been arguing about love since the beginning of civilization.

Whether you’re Adam and Eve, Christopher Columbus and Isabella, King Arthur and Guinevere, or just an ordinary couple sitting in Family Court, you’re probably going to have problems.

The only difference is that Bill and Carol get a judge who can take them on a tour through several thousand years of romantic dysfunction.

And only Troma would think that was a reasonable way to save a relationship.

items.title: Son Battle: Twisted Sister “We’re Not Gonna Take It” vs. Quiet Riot “Cum On Feel the Noize”
items.author: Schill
items.content:
Two enormous 1980s rock songs. Two giant choruses. Two videos that practically define the decade. And two songs that turned simple teenage rebellion into massive commercial success.

Twisted Sister’s “We’re Not Gonna Take It” and Quiet Riot’s “Cum On Feel the Noize” are both built around the same basic idea: turn the volume up and refuse to behave.

But they get there in very different ways.

“Cum On Feel the Noize” is a hard-rock party song originally written and recorded by Slade, with Quiet Riot transforming it into an enormous American metal hit in 1983. “We’re Not Gonna Take It” is Dee Snider’s own creation, released by Twisted Sister in 1984 and accompanied by one of the most memorable music videos of the decade.

One is swaggering and celebratory.

The other is defiant and confrontational.

One tells you to feel the noise.

The other tells you that you’ve had enough.

So let’s put them head-to-head.

Released in 1984 on Twisted Sister’s , “We’re Not Gonna Take It” became the band’s signature song and one of the defining hard-rock singles of the MTV era.

Dee Snider wrote the song around a straightforward message of rebellion. The verses build toward an enormous chorus in which the band essentially refuses to accept whatever authority is being imposed upon them.

The music itself is deceptively simple. The guitars are huge, the drums are direct and the chorus is designed for maximum audience participation.

Then there is Snider’s voice.

He doesn’t merely sing the chorus. He attacks it.

The song’s famous “Oh, we’re not gonna take it” refrain sounds like a crowd of thousands even when you’re hearing the studio recording.

The music video made the song even bigger. Inspired partly by and featuring actor Mark Metcalf as the increasingly exasperated father, the video turned the song’s rebellion into a comic mini-movie.

That combination of heavy metal, humor and a gigantic singalong chorus made “We’re Not Gonna Take It” almost impossible to forget.

Quiet Riot’s “Cum On Feel the Noize” arrived a year earlier and became a landmark moment for American heavy metal.

The song itself wasn’t new. Slade had originally released it in 1973 and had a major hit with it in the United Kingdom.

Quiet Riot’s version, however, introduced the song to a massive American audience.

Kevin DuBrow’s vocals are gritty and enthusiastic, while guitarist Carlos Cavazo gives the track its unmistakable metal punch. The band doesn’t radically rewrite the song’s basic structure. Instead, they turn it into something louder, heavier and perfectly suited to early-1980s American rock radio.

The chorus is the entire point.

And it practically demands that you yell along.

The success of “Cum On Feel the Noize” helped Quiet Riot’s become a massive commercial breakthrough and played an important role in bringing heavy metal further into the American mainstream.

“Cum On Feel the Noize” has a huge advantage in terms of proven songwriting because Noddy Holder and Jim Lea had already written an incredibly effective rock song for Slade.

The Quiet Riot version retains the basic structure that made the original work: verses that build toward an enormous chorus and a title that functions almost like an instruction to the audience.

But “We’re Not Gonna Take It” has something equally important.

It has a clear personality.

Dee Snider wrote a song that sounds exactly like its title. The entire composition revolves around defiance, and every musical element supports that message.

The songwriting isn’t complicated, but it is extremely efficient.

Winner: Twisted Sister – “We’re Not Gonna Take It”

Score: Twisted Sister 1 – Quiet Riot 0

Kevin DuBrow had one of the great voices of 1980s hard rock.

His delivery on “Cum On Feel the Noize” is raspy, energetic and slightly out of control in exactly the right way. He sounds like he’s having the time of his life.

Dee Snider approaches his song differently.

His voice is sharper and more theatrical. He knows how to build tension before unleashing the chorus, and there’s a sneering quality that fits the song’s rebellious attitude perfectly.

The most important thing is that both singers sound completely committed.

But Snider’s vocal performance is more distinctive.

Winner: Twisted Sister – “We’re Not Gonna Take It”

Score: Twisted Sister 2 – Quiet Riot 0

This is where Quiet Riot gets on the scoreboard.

Carlos Cavazo’s guitar work gives “Cum On Feel the Noize” considerably more of a traditional heavy-metal edge.

The riff is muscular and the overall guitar sound is thick and aggressive.

Twisted Sister’s guitar work is effective but more focused on supporting the chorus and keeping the song moving.

“We’re Not Gonna Take It” doesn’t need a guitar showcase.

But if we’re judging the guitars themselves, Quiet Riot has the heavier weapon.

Winner: Quiet Riot – “Cum On Feel the Noize”

Score: Twisted Sister 2 – Quiet Riot 1

Now we’re talking about two monster choruses.

“Cum On Feel the Noize” has a title that basically becomes a chant. The repeated phrase is impossible to forget, and Quiet Riot’s version makes it sound enormous.

But “We’re Not Gonna Take It” might have the more powerful audience-participation chorus.

The melody rises perfectly into the title phrase, and the repeated declaration makes the listener feel like they’re joining a rebellion.

You don’t merely hear the chorus.

Winner: Twisted Sister – “We’re Not Gonna Take It”

Score: Twisted Sister 3 – Quiet Riot 1

Quiet Riot’s production is a big reason “Cum On Feel the Noize” worked so well.

The guitars are thick, the drums hit hard and Kevin DuBrow’s vocal sits prominently in the mix. It sounds like a giant rock band without becoming completely muddy.

Twisted Sister’s production has a slightly different character.

“We’re Not Gonna Take It” is very polished, but the arrangement leaves plenty of room for the chorus to dominate. The guitars and drums provide a solid foundation while Snider remains the center of attention.

Quiet Riot sounds heavier.

Twisted Sister sounds more immediately accessible.

For pure hard-rock impact, Quiet Riot gets the edge.

Winner: Quiet Riot – “Cum On Feel the Noize”

Score: Twisted Sister 3 – Quiet Riot 2

This might be the most decisive round.

“Cum On Feel the Noize” received plenty of exposure during MTV’s golden era, but “We’re Not Gonna Take It” had something special.

The video turned the song into a story.

Mark Metcalf’s over-the-top father character became an instant comedy villain, while Dee Snider and the band represented the rebellious kids refusing to put up with his nonsense.

The video’s humor helped the song reach people who might not normally have been heavy-metal fans.

You could watch it once and remember it years later.

Winner: Twisted Sister – “We’re Not Gonna Take It”

Score: Twisted Sister 4 – Quiet Riot 2

Quiet Riot’s version of “Cum On Feel the Noize” is fantastic, but it is still a cover.

That doesn’t diminish the achievement. The band took an older glam-rock hit and completely transformed it for the American metal audience.

Still, Twisted Sister gets the advantage because “We’re Not Gonna Take It” is entirely their own statement.

The song has its own identity, its own attitude and its own visual world.

Winner: Twisted Sister – “We’re Not Gonna Take It”

Score: Twisted Sister 5 – Quiet Riot 2

Quiet Riot finally gets a chance to hit back hard.

“Cum On Feel the Noize” is absolutely explosive.

The song has that loose, sweaty, live-band quality that makes it feel like the audience is already going crazy before the first chorus arrives.

It isn’t trying to make a political statement.

It isn’t telling a complicated story.

It simply wants to make the room louder.

“We’re Not Gonna Take It” is energetic, but Quiet Riot’s track has a more primal rock-and-roll charge.

Winner: Quiet Riot – “Cum On Feel the Noize”

Score: Twisted Sister 5 – Quiet Riot 3

This is one of the most underrated differences between the two songs.

“Cum On Feel the Noize” has attitude, but much of its appeal comes from the band’s performance of a song that already existed.

“We’re Not Gonna Take It” feels inseparable from Dee Snider.

The song, the band, the video and Snider’s larger-than-life personality all became connected.

The song sounds like Twisted Sister.

That’s a powerful advantage.

Winner: Twisted Sister – “We’re Not Gonna Take It”

Score: Twisted Sister 6 – Quiet Riot 3

This is incredibly close.

“Cum On Feel the Noize” is practically designed for a party. The title tells everyone what they’re supposed to do, and the rhythm makes it almost impossible to sit still.

“We’re Not Gonna Take It” works too, but its rebellious message gives it a slightly different atmosphere.

If you’re throwing a giant 1980s rock party and want everybody yelling along, both songs are excellent.

Quiet Riot gets the narrow advantage because “Cum On Feel the Noize” feels like a celebration from beginning to end.

Winner: Quiet Riot – “Cum On Feel the Noize”

Score: Twisted Sister 6 – Quiet Riot 4

Both songs became important pieces of 1980s rock culture.

Quiet Riot’s “Cum On Feel the Noize” was a major American breakthrough and helped demonstrate that heavy metal could become enormous on mainstream radio and MTV.

“Metal Health” became a landmark commercial success, and Quiet Riot helped open the door for the wave of metal bands that followed.

Twisted Sister’s impact was different.

“We’re Not Gonna Take It” became a pop-culture shorthand for rebellion. The video was enormously memorable, and the song eventually became associated with everything from teenage independence to political protests and sporting events.

The phrase itself became bigger than the song.

Winner: Twisted Sister – “We’re Not Gonna Take It”

Score: Twisted Sister 7 – Quiet Riot 4

This is another difficult one.

“Cum On Feel the Noize” has enormous replay value because it’s so immediately enjoyable. You don’t have to think about it. The guitars kick in, DuBrow starts singing and you’re ready to go.

“We’re Not Gonna Take It” has that same instant accessibility, but the video and chorus add another layer of nostalgia.

There’s also something about the song’s simplicity that makes it difficult to wear out.

You can hear the opening and immediately know exactly what is coming.

And you’re probably going to sing along anyway.

Winner: Twisted Sister – “We’re Not Gonna Take It”

Final Score: Twisted Sister 8 – Quiet Riot 4

Twisted Sister – “We’re Not Gonna Take It”: 8

Quiet Riot – “Cum On Feel the Noize”: 4

Winner: Twisted Sister – “We’re Not Gonna Take It”

Quiet Riot absolutely deserves credit for putting “Cum On Feel the Noize” on the map for an enormous American audience. Their version is louder, heavier and more aggressive than Slade’s original, and Kevin DuBrow’s performance gives it tremendous personality.

It’s one of those songs that can instantly turn a room into a rock concert.

But Twisted Sister’s “We’re Not Gonna Take It” wins because it offers more than just a great hard-rock performance.

It has an unforgettable video.

It has one of the biggest singalong choruses of the decade.

And most importantly, it has an identity that belongs completely to Twisted Sister.

Quiet Riot tells you to .

Twisted Sister tells you that you’ve finally had enough.

That distinction gives “We’re Not Gonna Take It” the advantage.

It’s not necessarily the heavier song.

It’s not necessarily the more technically impressive song.

But as an all-around piece of 1980s rock culture, it’s nearly impossible to beat.

The moment that chorus hits, the audience doesn’t just listen.

“We’re not gonna take it!”

And suddenly everybody in the room is part of the rebellion.

items.title: Sunday Weird History Lesson: The Man Who Declared War on the Moon
items.author: Schill
items.content:
There is something wonderfully absurd about the idea of declaring war on the Moon.

It isn’t a country. It doesn’t have a government. It doesn’t have an army. It doesn’t even belong to anyone.

At least, that’s what most people would assume.

Dennis Hope had a different idea.

In the 1980s, Hope, an American entrepreneur from Nevada, discovered what he believed was a loophole in international law that allowed him to claim ownership of extraterrestrial real estate. He eventually began selling plots of land on the Moon to customers around the world.

He didn’t literally declare war on the Moon, despite the colorful way the story is sometimes told. His real claim was considerably stranger:

And he wasn’t stopping with the Moon.

Hope also claimed large portions of Mars, Venus and Mercury, turning himself into one of the most unusual property entrepreneurs of the modern era.

The story is part legal experiment, part business venture, part publicity stunt—and entirely bizarre.

The Moon Needs a Landlord

Dennis Hope’s story began with a personal financial problem.

According to accounts of his business, Hope was going through a difficult period in his life in the late 1970s and early 1980s. He began thinking about ways to make money and eventually became interested in an obscure area of international law.

The answer seemed obvious.

The United States had landed astronauts there. The Soviet Union had sent spacecraft. Other countries had photographed it, studied it and sent probes toward it.

But no country had officially claimed the Moon as its own.

Hope started examining the legal agreements governing outer space and noticed language concerning national governments claiming territory in space.

His interpretation was that these restrictions applied to nations, not necessarily private individuals.

That was the opening he was looking for.

The central document in Hope’s argument was the 1967 Outer Space Treaty.

The treaty established the principle that celestial bodies such as the Moon should not become the territory of individual nations.

Governments could not simply plant a flag on the Moon and declare:

“Congratulations, everyone. We own this now.”

The treaty also established that outer space and celestial bodies were to be used for peaceful purposes and that they were not subject to national appropriation.

Hope interpreted this differently.

He argued that while governments were prohibited from claiming celestial territory, the treaty did not explicitly prevent an individual from doing so.

So he filed paperwork claiming ownership.

The logic was unconventional.

The consequences were even more unconventional.

Or at least, he believed he did.

Selling Lunar Real Estate

Having claimed the Moon, Hope faced a practical question.

What do you do with a Moon?

His answer was surprisingly capitalist.

Hope established the Lunar Embassy, a business that marketed lunar property to customers.

People could purchase certificates claiming ownership of plots of land on the Moon.

Depending on the package, buyers could receive maps, certificates and other documentation identifying their supposed lunar property.

Suddenly, ordinary people could become extraterrestrial landowners.

A person who couldn’t afford a house on Earth could theoretically own several acres on the Moon.

The idea was irresistible.

It combined the novelty of space exploration with the familiar language of real estate.

Instead of buying a vacation property in Florida, you could buy property overlooking a lunar crater.

There was just one minor problem.

The World’s Most Inaccessible Real Estate

Buying land is generally considered more useful when you can actually visit it.

Moon property had an obvious disadvantage.

There were no utility connections.

There wasn’t even a reliable way to send a moving truck.

A lunar homeowner couldn’t call a contractor and say, “I’d like a two-bedroom house built next Saturday.”

Even today, decades after Hope began selling lunar property, private citizens cannot simply travel to the Moon and inspect their real estate.

That didn’t stop people from buying.

The novelty was the point.

A lunar property certificate made for a memorable gift, conversation piece or novelty purchase.

It was less like buying a suburban backyard and more like buying a tiny piece of humanity’s future.

Millions of Lunar Homeowners

Hope’s business attracted customers from around the world.

According to claims associated with the Lunar Embassy, millions of people have purchased extraterrestrial property through the company.

Whether those buyers actually obtained legally enforceable property rights is a completely different question.

The certificates certainly gave customers something tangible.

They could hold a document saying that they owned a particular parcel of the Moon.

But possessing a certificate isn’t necessarily the same thing as possessing a legally recognized property title.

That distinction becomes extremely important when dealing with real estate located approximately 240,000 miles away.

Can Anyone Actually Own the Moon?

This is where the story gets complicated.

The Outer Space Treaty is widely regarded as establishing that nations cannot claim sovereignty over celestial bodies.

But private property rights in space are a much more complicated subject.

Hope’s interpretation has never become an internationally recognized system of lunar property ownership.

There is no global government that has officially recognized his claim.

No major space agency treats his property maps as authoritative.

And there is no lunar land registry accepting applications for backyard swimming pools.

In practical terms, buying one of Hope’s certificates doesn’t give someone an internationally recognized piece of lunar territory in the same way that buying a house on Earth gives you legally enforceable property rights.

That hasn’t stopped the business from continuing.

The Moon Doesn’t Send Lawyers

One reason the scheme is so entertaining is that it exposes the enormous gap between legal theory and physical reality.

Imagine trying to enforce your lunar property rights.

Someone lands on your property.

And suppose the person refuses to leave.

You have a trespasser on the Moon.

The problem becomes even more complicated because there is no universally accepted lunar government capable of enforcing ordinary property law.

Earth has spent thousands of years developing systems for buying, selling, taxing and defending land.

The Moon doesn’t have any of that.

The Business Became a Cultural Phenomenon

Regardless of the legal arguments, Hope understood something important about human psychology.

People love the idea of owning something extraordinary.

Space has always had enormous cultural appeal.

The Apollo missions transformed the Moon from a distant object in the night sky into a place humans could actually visit.

Hope took that fascination and turned it into a commercial product.

For a relatively small amount of money, a customer could tell friends:

“I own land on the Moon.”

That sentence alone was worth something.

It was a great conversation starter.

It was an unusual birthday present.

It was a piece of space-age memorabilia.

And for some customers, it may have represented something more philosophical—a symbolic connection to humanity’s future beyond Earth.

Hope Didn’t Stop With the Moon

Hope expanded his extraterrestrial real estate empire to other planets.

He claimed large portions of Mars, Mercury and Venus.

He also sold property packages associated with these worlds.

The idea became increasingly surreal.

A customer could potentially own a piece of the Moon, Mars or another celestial body without ever leaving Earth.

In a way, Hope created the world’s most speculative real estate market.

There were no open houses.

No photographs of the kitchen.

No school district ratings.

No neighborhood association.

And absolutely no chance of driving by to see whether the previous owner had left junk in the garage.

The strangest question is whether these purchases could ever become useful.

Imagine that lunar settlements become common in the future.

Suppose humans eventually establish permanent cities on the Moon.

What happens to Hope’s customers?

Could someone show up at a lunar settlement with a decades-old certificate and say:

That’s where the uncertainty becomes enormous.

Future governments and international organizations would have to determine how lunar resources and territory are governed.

They may create entirely new systems for habitation, scientific research, mining and settlement.

There is no guarantee that a certificate purchased from a private company today would have any legal standing under those future systems.

In other words, lunar property buyers are betting on a legal future that hasn’t been written yet.

So how did a man selling Moon real estate become associated with the idea of declaring war on the Moon?

The answer is mostly storytelling.

Hope didn’t actually assemble an army.

He didn’t send tanks toward the Sea of Tranquility.

He didn’t fire missiles at the lunar surface.

He didn’t stand outside a government building and announce hostilities against Earth’s satellite.

His real achievement was considerably stranger.

He looked at a celestial body that humanity had admired for thousands of years and asked:

That’s what makes the story so memorable.

The Ultimate Real Estate Pitch

Dennis Hope’s lunar property scheme sits somewhere between entrepreneurship, legal interpretation and science-fiction fantasy.

Critics can argue that his interpretation of international space law doesn’t establish genuine ownership.

They can point out that no internationally recognized authority has validated his lunar real estate claims.

They can laugh at the idea of selling land that nobody can currently visit.

All of those objections are reasonable.

But Hope still accomplished something remarkable.

He turned an abstract legal question into a business.

He took something that had always seemed completely outside the real estate market—the Moon—and gave it addresses, maps, certificates and customers.

He transformed lunar land into a product.

The story of Dennis Hope is ultimately less about whether someone actually owns the Moon and more about the extraordinary things people will buy when imagination, technology and commerce collide.

Human beings have always wanted to own unusual things.

People collect meteorites.

They buy pieces of historic buildings.

They purchase celebrity memorabilia.

Hope simply took the idea one enormous step further.

He offered people the chance to own a piece of another world.

Maybe the certificates will someday become valuable historical curiosities.

Maybe future lunar governments will completely ignore them.

Maybe humanity will eventually build cities on the Moon and discover that the entire concept of extraterrestrial real estate needs to be reinvented.

Or maybe lunar property will remain exactly what it is today: a fascinating novelty that allows someone to look up at the night sky and say, with a straight face:

Dennis Hope never actually declared war on the Moon.

He did something much stranger.
